messages.subject: Why Deducer
parts:
Hello fellow Miners

I am a practicing Data Analyst for approximately 3 years now. I have
already used a variety of tools, but regarding the number of existent
data mining tools / environments etc. only a small portion. After
reading the news on the r-packages mailing list my first thought was:
"another one ?"

To reduce the complexity of the question: What distinguishes Deducer
from Rattle (http://rattle.togaware.com/) and what makes it the better
choice ?

kind regards,

Steffen

messages.author: 267c7c6c510dc8a2
messages.subject: Re: Why Deducer
parts:
Steffen,

First off, Deducer is primarily targeted at data analysis rather
than data mining, though obviously there is a lot of overlap there. I
haven't really used rattle, but it looks like useful program.

At first glance here are my thoughts regarding the advantages of Deducer:
1. I'm not particularly enamored by the way that interaction with the
data is done in rattle (going back and forth from the data tab to
specify new targets and inputs). Only one dataset allowed at a time.
2. I'll leave it to you to decide if the UI is easier in general.
3. Deducer has a fairly advanced system to analyze contingency tables
4. Deducer has an easily usable data viewer/editor
5. Deducer is integrated into the console. No new window or special
logs. You will hardly know it's there unless you are using it.
6. It doesn't appear that rattle allows for interactions in their
lm/glm models. I couldn't use a tool that didn't let me put
interactions into a model.
7. rattle does have variable transformations (which deducer doesn't
have yet, but doesn't have much in the way of other data manipulation
subseting, recoding, and merging.

Give it a try and let me know what you think.

Ian

Hi Steffen,
IMO maybe it wasn't really the right question, although you
certainly have the freedom to ask.

I come from about 12 years of using primarily Gentoo Linux as my
desktop and hence have a lot of Open Source experience. I'm not a
software developer but have participated on a lot of OS projects
helping with testing, interfaces, comparison with closed source
feature sets, etc. My thought is that it is ALWAYS a benefit to have
more programs available.

1) Even if programs do exactly the same thing - and I don't think that
applies to Deducer and Rattle - we still benefit from having access to
different views of how to accomplish the same things. Often we find
improvements in the GUIs, etc., in doing this.

2) Over time Open Source programs and the developers that support them
come and go. I consider it healthy that there are alternatives.

3) In the Pro Audio area there has been a lot of benefit from having
many big, complicated programs that do similar things, like recording,
mixing and mastering music. While these programs all essentially
produce the same final product - data for a CD - there has been a lot
of HEALTHY competition which has made all the programs that have
survived better, not worse. When OS developers see an interesting
feature in one program they are naturally driven to add features that
are identical or better. Often these developers actually work together
instead of anti-competitively like would happen between different
for-pay software companies.

So, my input is 'the more the merrier'. It's good, not bad!

Cheers,
Mark

P.S. - Even though I'm on OS advocate I'm actually playing with
Deducer on my Win Vista machine.

messages.author: 267c7c6c510dc8a2
messages.subject: Re: Why Deducer
parts:
Good suggestion.

Let me start off by saying that I really like what Dr. Fox has done. He has created a great resource for beginners to get familiar with R. Rcmdr is designed as an interface for beginners, and it is Dr. Fox's hope that they will be "weened of of the dialogs" and eventually just use the command line. I have a bit of a different goal with Deducer. I want Deducer to be user friendly enough to be used by someone just starting out, yet flexible and powerful enough to increase the efficiency of expert users. It would be unfair to criticize Rcmdr for not serving the needs of advanced users, because it was never designed for this. That said, I think Deducer has a lot of advantages, both in ease of use, and increased efficiency.

Ease of use:
1. Console integration: It is a bit awkward to have a separate console for the menus as Rcmdr has. Deducer is fully integrated into the usual windows console, though it is best used with the user friendly cross-platform JGR console.
2. Data viewer: Beginners really like to be able to see their data. The data viewer goes a long way in helping them see what they are doing.
3. Task based dialogs: Deducer has task based dialogs instead of function based ones. Rcmdr has separate dialogs for each R function it uses. For example, there are 6 menu items for loading data from a file (one for each loading function), whereas Deducer has one which picks the right function based on extension and user selection. As another example, two-sample tests in Deducer are all grouped into one dialog because they are all different ways of answering the same question.
4. Help system: Deducer's online help system walks the user through the dialogs with screen shots and practical examples.
5. Prettier interface: The toolkit that is used to make Rcmdr is somewhat limiting, and (IMHO) doesn't have the nicest look and feel.
6. Drag and drop: Deducer implements drag and drop to and from the dialog lists.

Efficiency:
1. Dialogs have memory: One of the constantly vexing things about Rcmdr is that the dialogs do not remember what options were selected the last time they were used. Data analysis is an iterative process, it is very rare that I specify exactly the right set of options the first time.
2. Multiple datasets: Deducer can work with multiple data frames at the same time. No need to specify an "active set." Deducer automatically defaults the variable selector to the most recently used dataset, but this can be changed easily for each analysis.
3. Multiple analyses: sometimes you'll want to do a t-test on 5 variables. In Rcmdr, you have to go through the dialog 5 times.

Both:
1. Result tables: tests and analyses are formatted into easy to read tables. This is particularly apparent when comparing the two-programs' implementations of contingency tables.
2. Analysis plots: Each analysis has at least one descriptive plot which helps users visualize their results, and identify potential problems such as outliers/non-normality.

Areas where Rcmdr is superior:
1. Plug-in API: Rcmdr has a nice plug-in api, allowing developers to extend and alter it to their preferences. The next version of Deducer will have this.
2. Plots: Deducer has no dialogs for creating plots (outside of the analysis menu). The next version of Deducer will rectify this.
3. Richer set of analyses: Rcmdr is more mature, and thus has a more rich set of analyses that have been programmed into it, including many excellent plug-ins.
